title: Shapiro's Cyclic Inequality for n = 4, with a Two-Parameter Equality Locus
description: Nesbitt's inequality is the n = 3 case of Shapiro's cyclic inequality Σ aᵢ/(aᵢ₊₁ + aᵢ₊₂) ≥ n/2. This entry settles the next case, n = 4: for positive reals a, b, c, d, a/(b+c) + b/(c+d) + c/(d+a) + d/(a+b) ≥ 2. The engine is the two-term Titu (Engel-form Cauchy–Schwarz) estimate p²/x + q²/y ≥ (p+q)²/(x+y), whose deficit is the explicit square (py − qx)²/(xy(x+y)). Pairing the opposite terms (1,3) and (2,4) and applying Titu twice folds the four fractions down to a single quotient (a+b+c+d)²/(X+Y), and the polynomial identity (a+b+c+d)² = 2(X+Y) + (a−c)² + (b−d)² exhibits the whole deficit, giving the sharp bound Σ ≥ 2 + ((a−c)² + (b−d)²)/(X+Y). Unlike Nesbitt's single diagonal a = b = c, the n = 4 equality locus is the genuinely two-parameter family {a = c, b = d} (e.g. (1,2,1,2) gives Σ = 2), which we characterise as an iff.

overview.historicalContext: Harold Shapiro proposed in 1954 (American Mathematical Monthly) the cyclic inequality Σ aᵢ/(aᵢ₊₁ + aᵢ₊₂) ≥ n/2 for positive reals. It turned out to be subtle: the inequality is true for n ≤ 12 even and n ≤ 23 odd, and false beyond (counterexamples exist for n = 14 even and n = 25 odd, by Lighthill, Rankin, and others). Nesbitt's 1903 inequality is exactly the n = 3 instance. The n = 4 case treated here is the first step into the genuinely cyclic regime, where — unlike n = 3 — the minimum is attained on a positive-dimensional set rather than a single ray.
overview.problemStatement:
For positive reals a, b, c, d, is a/(b+c) + b/(c+d) + c/(d+a) + d/(a+b) always at least 2, and when is it exactly 2?

**Answer: Yes**, the sum is ≥ 2, with equality **iff a = c and b = d**. The defect from 2 equals an explicit nonnegative quantity ((a−c)² + (b−d)²)/(X+Y), zero precisely on the family a = c, b = d.
overview.text: The 4-cycle Shapiro sum a/(b+c) + b/(c+d) + c/(d+a) + d/(a+b) of a positive 4-tuple is bounded below by 2, attained exactly when a = c and b = d.
overview.proofStrategy: Write each term a/(b+c) = a²/(a(b+c)) and pair the opposite terms: (1,3) gives, by the two-term Titu estimate engel2, a/(b+c) + c/(d+a) ≥ (a+c)²/X with X = a(b+c) + c(d+a); (2,4) gives b/(c+d) + d/(a+b) ≥ (b+d)²/Y with Y = b(c+d) + d(a+b). A third Titu application folds (a+c)²/X + (b+d)²/Y ≥ (a+b+c+d)²/(X+Y). Finally the polynomial identity (a+b+c+d)² = 2(X+Y) + (a−c)² + (b−d)² rewrites the single quotient as 2 + ((a−c)² + (b−d)²)/(X+Y), giving the sharp deficit bound; nonnegativity yields the inequality. For the equality case, Σ = 2 forces the squared deficit term to vanish, hence (a−c)² + (b−d)² = 0 and a = c, b = d; conversely a = c, b = d collapses every estimate to equality.
keyInsights: The two-term Cauchy–Schwarz (Titu/Engel) estimate has an exact square deficit (py − qx)²/(xy(x+y)), so all inequalities here are equalities-minus-an-explicit-square — a self-certifying SOS-style proof
Pairing the OPPOSITE terms (1,3) and (2,4), not adjacent ones, is what makes the 4-cycle telescope cleanly into a single (a+b+c+d)² numerator
The folding identity (a+b+c+d)² = 2(X+Y) + (a−c)² + (b−d)² turns the whole deficit into two squares, simultaneously delivering the bound and the equality locus
The minimum is attained on the two-parameter family a = c, b = d — a structural departure from the n = 3 (Nesbitt) case where only a = b = c achieves equality

The opposite pairing (1,3)/(2,4) is forced by the cyclic structure, not an arbitrary choice: rotating indices by 2 (i ↦ i+2 mod 4) is an involution of the 4-cycle that swaps term 1 with term 3 and term 2 with term 4 while fixing the sum; grouping by this involution's orbits is exactly what lets the two Titu applications recombine into a single (a+b+c+d)² numerator, whereas an adjacent pairing like (1,2)/(3,4) does not respect any symmetry of the sum and would not collapse as cleanly

sections.title: Shapiro's Inequality for n = 4
sections.summary: Nonnegativity of the deficit term gives a/(b+c) + b/(c+d) + c/(d+a) + d/(a+b) ≥ 2.

sections.title: Two-Parameter Equality Locus
sections.summary: Σ = 2 iff a = c and b = d; the squared deficit forces both differences to zero, and conversely the family a = c, b = d attains the bound — a positive-dimensional minimiser set unlike Nesbitt's single point.

crossReferences.description: Nesbitt's inequality is the n = 3 case of the same Shapiro cyclic family; this entry proves the n = 4 case and contrasts the equality loci (single diagonal a = b = c for n = 3 versus the two-parameter family a = c, b = d for n = 4).
The proof engine is the two-term Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in Engel (Titu) form, here established directly through its exact square deficit rather than via a named Mathlib lemma.

conclusion.summary: Shapiro's cyclic inequality for n = 4, a/(b+c) + b/(c+d) + c/(d+a) + d/(a+b) ≥ 2, is machine-checked with 0 axioms via two applications of the Engel-form Cauchy–Schwarz estimate and a folding identity, which also yields the sharp deficit and the equality characterisation a = c ∧ b = d.
conclusion.implications: Beyond Nesbitt (n = 3), the n = 4 case already exhibits a positive-dimensional minimiser set, showing that the equality structure of Shapiro's inequality changes qualitatively with n. The opposite-pairing + Titu-folding template, with its explicit square deficits, is a reusable certified route for even cyclic sums.
openQuestions: Does the opposite-pairing + Titu folding extend to n = 6 (a valid Shapiro case) to give a certified deficit, or does the absence of a clean two-block pairing for n ≥ 6 require a different SOS certificate?
Characterise the full equality locus of Shapiro's inequality for each valid even n; is it always the 'alternating-equal' family aᵢ = aᵢ₊₂?
